lead.headline: Risk Roars Back Over Thanksgiving: Europe Jumps 2%, Seoul and São Paulo Soar and Nasdaq Futures Climb 2.4%, While Gulf Attacks Lift Brent to $96.57
lead.dek: With Wall Street shut, the DAX rose about 2.1% and Milan 2.4% on Thursday, Brazil's Ibovespa had its best day since October with a 6.1% jump and the Kospi was up as much as 3.6% on Friday; Brent's expiring January contract settled at $96.57 after a Houthi strike on Aramco's Jazan refinery and new Iranian mine claims near Hormuz, and Tokyo core inflation hit a 16-month high.
body: Europe used the US holiday to undo two days of losses. Germany's DAX ended about 2.1% higher near 25,216 (end-of-day quote), the FTSE 100 gained 1.75% to 10,609.30, the CAC 40 1.61% to 8,108.74 and Milan's FTSE MIB 2.36% to 48,362.35, with every IBEX 35 member higher in a 2.26% advance (26 Nov close). Banks and chipmakers led, Stellantis rose almost 9%, Imperial Brands had its best day since 1999 (+13%) after Altria said it was weighing a cash offer, and Babcock gained 6.5% on an £8.7 billion submarine contract. Strategists quoted in Paris cautioned that thin volumes limit what the bounce says.

The relief spread to emerging markets. Brazil's Ibovespa jumped 6.07% to 176,799.84 on 26 Nov after mid-November IPCA-15 inflation came in at 0.22% against forecasts near 0.36% and on reports that Bradesco chairman Luiz Carlos Trabuco could become finance minister; Tel Aviv's TA-125 rose 2.95%. On Friday the Kospi was up 3.57% at 4,879.25 by early afternoon and the Kosdaq 6.34%, as foreigners bought about 1 trillion won and Seoul called an emergency market-stabilisation meeting for 30 Nov; the Nikkei was 1.17% higher at 58,172 at the lunch break after Tokyo core CPI rose to 2.9%. India was steadier, with the Sensex up 0.46% to 84,328.59 on an 18th straight day of foreign buying, while Vietnam's VN-Index fell 3.42% on the proposed 35% US tariff (26 Nov close).

US index futures rose in Asian hours on Friday, with Nasdaq-100 futures up about 2.4% and S&P 500 futures about 1.7%, ahead of a half-day session that closes at 19:00 CET. The last cash closes are Wednesday's: S&P 500 7,182.78, Nasdaq 23,585.80, Dow 50,182.95. The 10-year Treasury yield was quoted near 4.91% in holiday trade, about 7bp above Wednesday's close, with a 9 December Fed hike still almost fully priced.

Oil carried the war premium higher. Brent's January contract settled $1.96 (2.07%) higher at $96.57 on 26 Nov, a third straight gain; it expires on 30 Nov, and the February contract traded about $4.20 lower. A projectile blamed on the Houthis hit Saudi Aramco's 400,000-barrel-a-day Jazan refinery, killing a worker and halting some units, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers hit mines near Oman's Khasab (unverified), and Kuwait blamed Iranian drone debris for two deaths. Gold rose about 1.9% to near $3,630 and silver almost 5% in Asian trade on Friday. OPEC+ ministers meet on Sunday.

impact.title: What it means for markets
points: The rebound came on thin holiday volumes, so Friday's half-day US session is the first real test of whether Wednesday's intraday reversal holds; the VIX was still 28.29 at Wednesday's close.

Oil's war premium now reflects attacks on Saudi energy plants, not only shipping. The roughly $4 gap between January and February Brent shows the market pricing an acute near-term squeeze more than a lasting one, with OPEC+ meeting on 29 Nov.

Global tightening stays the backdrop: a December Fed hike is almost fully priced, the ECB minutes were read as a hint of a December move, traders put BoE hike odds near 91% and Tokyo inflation keeps a BoJ hike in view. That has favoured banks in the rebound and weighs on long-duration assets.
Tariff risk is being priced country by country: Vietnam fell 3.4% on its proposed 35% rate while Korea, Taiwan and Japan, near their existing 15% caps, rallied.

read.title: The Ledger's Read
paragraphs: Thursday was a reminder of how much a market without its anchor can move. With New York shut, Europe, Brazil, Tel Aviv and on Friday Seoul staged outsized rebounds, helped by short covering after two bruising sessions and by the fact that Wednesday's US reversal had already shown buyers waiting below. Thin volumes flatter such moves, and several strategists said as much. The first real verdict comes in Friday's shortened US session, where Nasdaq-100 futures were already pricing a gain of more than 2% in Asian trade.

The rally did not remove the two forces that have driven the past fortnight: tightening central banks and a war premium in energy. A December Fed hike is all but priced, the ECB minutes read hawkish, sterling markets put BoE hike odds above 90% and Tokyo's 2.9% core inflation keeps the BoJ on track. Oil is the more unpredictable channel: the Houthis are now striking Saudi refineries, Iran claims more mine hits near Hormuz, and Brent's front month rose to $96.57. The steep discount of the February contract suggests traders see the squeeze as acute rather than permanent, which makes Sunday's OPEC+ meetings and the 30 Nov expiry worth watching.

What to watch: the US half-day session and Black Friday retail read-through today, the Tata Trusts hearing in Mumbai, OPEC+ on 29 Nov, India's GDP and Korea's stabilisation meeting on 30 Nov, Jensen Huang's congressional appearances from 1 Dec, and the RBI on 4 Dec ahead of the Fed on 8-9 Dec. Tariff risk is being priced country by country, with Vietnam the clearest loser so far.

stories.headline: Wall Street Set for a Holiday Bounce: Nasdaq-100 Futures Jump 2.4% Ahead of Friday's Half-Day Session
stories.summary: US stock futures rallied in Asian hours on Friday 27 Nov, with Nasdaq-100 futures up about 2.4% and S&P 500 futures about 1.7%, as reported by investingLive, after cash markets stayed shut for Thanksgiving on 26 Nov. The last cash closes date from Wednesday 25 Nov: S&P 500 7,182.78 (-0.25%), Nasdaq Composite 23,585.80 (-0.62%) and Dow 50,182.95 (+0.33%), after the S&P 500 had been down as much as 3.2% and the Nasdaq 4.6% intraday. Futures had already firmed on Thursday, about 0.3% for the S&P 500, while Europe and Asia rebounded. Friday's session ends early at 1 p.m. ET, and the 10-year Treasury yield was quoted about 7bp higher near 4.91%.
stories.market: A 1.7% S&P 500 futures gain would put the index back near 7,300 at the open if it holds; thin Black Friday volumes can exaggerate moves, and chip names (Nvidia, Micron) are the swing factor after this week's swings.

body: US equity futures pointed to a strong reopening on Friday 27 Nov. The rebound in futures follows a volatile Wednesday 25 Nov, when the S&P 500 recovered from a 3.2% intraday fall to close down 0.25% at 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq Composite trimmed a 4.6% slide to a 0.62% loss at 23,585.80, while the Dow ended 0.33% higher at 50,182.95.

Overseas markets set the tone during the US holiday: Europe's main indices rose roughly 1.6% to 2.4% on 26 Nov as investors read proposed US tariffs on the EU as likely capped at the 15% agreed last year, and Asian chip stocks extended their rebound on Friday, with Korea's Kospi up close to 3%.

Friday is a shortened session, with stocks closing at 1 p.m. ET. Treasury yields were quoted about 7bp higher, with the 10-year near 4.91%, as markets continued to price an almost certain Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 Dec.

Milan's FTSE MIB led with a 2.36% gain to 48,362.35. Banks and technology led: Deutsche Bank rose 3% early and the STOXX 600 was up 1.4% at 634.94 by 08:15 GMT. Reuters reported reassurance that proposed US duties on the EU would likely be capped at the 15% agreed last year. Analysts warned that thin Thanksgiving volumes made the move fragile.
stories.market: Autos (Stellantis +8.9%), chips (Soitec, STMicro) and banks led the recovery; the euro was little changed near $1.0975, so the rally was not a currency story.

body: Europe recovered much of the week's losses on Thursday. The DAX ended about 2.08% higher near 25,216, after closing at 24,702 on 25 Nov; the FTSE 100 rose 182.36 points to 10,609.30; the CAC 40 gained 1.61% to 8,108.74 with 39 of its 40 members higher; and Milan's FTSE MIB added 2.36%.

The pan-European STOXX 600 was up 1.4% at 634.94 early in the session, according to Reuters, after falling more than 1% on Wednesday on worries about US inflation, higher rates, trade and AI-driven growth. Signs that US duties on the EU would likely stay at the agreed 15% cap helped sentiment.

Banks and technology led. Deutsche Bank and Standard Chartered gained early, and HSBC and Barclays closed more than 2% higher in London. Chipmakers Soitec and STMicroelectronics rose about 7% and 4.5%, while Stellantis jumped 8.9% and Renault 5.7%. London also got a lift from Imperial Brands, up about 13% on Altria's interest, and Babcock's £8.7 billion submarine contract.
Analysts were cautious. Joachim Klement of Panmure Liberum said it was unclear why investors had bought the dip, and John Plassard of Cité Gestion warned that low volumes limit what the move signals.

stories.summary: The ECB's minutes, published on 26 Nov, were read by Rabobank as a clear hint of a December rate increase, with economist Bas van Geffen seeing a pause after next month as most likely. In London, traders priced a 91.4% chance of a 25bp Bank of England hike in December, according to LSEG data, as the BoE warned that risks in the financial system have grown, citing the Middle East war and heavy borrowing by AI companies and governments. In Tokyo, November core inflation rose to 2.9%, and markets expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates to 1.5% at its 17-18 Dec meeting.
stories.market: Expected hikes in Europe and Japan are narrowing rate gaps with the US, but the euro (near $1.0975) and yen (near 159.2) barely moved, as the Fed is also expected to tighten.

body: The ECB's account of its last meeting, released on 26 Nov, kept options open but, in Rabobank's reading, gave a clear hint of another hike in December. Bas van Geffen said a pause after that move currently looks most likely.

The Bank of England said risks in the global financial system had increased in recent months, tying them to the Middle East conflict, which it said is lifting inflation and interest rates, and to heavy borrowing by AI companies and governments. Traders priced a 91.4% chance of a 25bp December increase, according to LSEG data reported by Reuters. Sterling traded around 0.7634 per dollar.

In Japan, November Tokyo core CPI rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, just below the 3.0% forecast, while the measure that also excludes energy eased to 2.5%. Markets expect a hike to 1.5% on 17-18 Dec, and the two-year JGB yield was near 1.76%.

That was the expiring January contract, which ends trading on 30 Nov; the February contract, which many outlets already quote, traded about $4.20 lower, around $92-93. stories.market: Higher crude helps energy stocks and producer currencies but adds to inflation pressure and rate-hike bets, and is a headwind for importers such as India.

stories.headline: Democrats Who Take Over Congress in January Vow to Fight the New Section 301 Tariffs, as Yale Puts the Average US Rate Back Near Its Pre-Ruling Level
stories.summary: A day after the US Trade Representative proposed Section 301 overcapacity tariffs on 14 economies, Democrats who won both chambers on 3 Nov said they would challenge them: Senator Ron Wyden, expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, called the plan an attempt to rebuild tariffs the Supreme Court struck down, and Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be House Speaker, pledged to stop them (26 Nov). Trade Representative Jamieson Greer described the changes as minor top-ups. The Yale Budget Lab estimates the proposals would lift the average US statutory tariff rate from 11.4% to 13.9%, close to the 13.8% in place before the February ruling. No duty is yet in force: comments are due 5 Jan 2027, hearings start 25 Jan 2027 and no effective date has been set, though implementation is widely expected early in 2027.
stories.market: With US markets shut on 26 Nov and trading only a half-day on 27 Nov, the first US equity read comes today; Capital Economics argues the duties mostly replace July's forced-labour tariffs but should keep core goods inflation firm into 2027, a factor for Treasury yields and Fed pricing.

body: The proposals, published on 25 Nov after an eight-month investigation, set tariffs of 15% for the EU and up to 15% for Japan, Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan, up to 18% for five South and Southeast Asian economies, up to 20% for China and Singapore, up to 25% for India and up to 35% for Vietnam, with Mexico and Norway left undetermined. USTR says it reviewed roughly 1,070 public comments and heard nearly 140 witnesses (Political.org, 26 Nov).

The political backdrop has shifted since the probes began in March. Democrats won majorities in both the House and Senate on 3 Nov and take control when the new Congress convenes in January 2027, the same month the tariff hearings open. Wyden and Jeffries both framed the plan as a workaround of the Supreme Court's February ruling that the emergency-powers law did not authorise the earlier tariffs; neither has yet set out a specific legislative route (as of 26 Nov).

Greer has played down the scale of the change, calling the new rates top-ups, while Georgetown law professor Gregory Shaffer described the use of Section 301 as cynical (TL;DR Daily News, 26 Nov). The Yale Budget Lab's estimate of an average statutory rate of 13.9%, up from 11.4%, implies the administration would recover almost all of the tariff level lost in February.

Capital Economics chief economist Stephen Brown said the duties are less alarming than they look because they largely replace the July forced-labour tariffs and do not stack on them, but still expects them to keep core goods inflation firm into next year (AP, 26 Nov). Goods already under Section 232 tariffs, including semiconductors, cars and steel, are exempt in the 13 non-China proposals.

On China, the AP reports that Washington and Beijing extended their trade truce by two months to 10 Jan 2027 and agreed reciprocal tariff cuts on non-sensitive goods worth about $60 billion; China's commerce ministry nonetheless called the 301 move unilateral and said it reserves the right to respond (26 Nov).

stories.headline: Tokyo Lodges a Protest, Jakarta Sees an Edge Over Vietnam, and Beijing's Commerce Ministry Calls the US Tariffs Unilateral
stories.summary: Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said on 26 Nov that Japan has no structural excess capacity and that Tokyo had conveyed its objection to Washington over a proposed tariff of up to 15%. Indonesia, facing up to 18% (25% if talks fail), struck a different tone: an economy-ministry spokesman said the gap with rivals such as Vietnam (up to 35%) could favour Indonesian textiles, footwear, metal products and renewable components, and the foreign ministry stressed on 27 Nov that the rate is only a proposal. Thailand called its 18% cap better than expected and Malaysia denied any market-distorting overcapacity, while China's commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong called the move unilateral, said it breaks WTO rules and reserved the right to respond (26 Nov).
stories.market: The rupiah weakened 0.67% to 18,348 per dollar and Indonesia's 10-year yield slipped 1.6bp to 7.696% (26 Nov, as reported 27 Nov); the relative tariff gaps matter most for apparel, footwear and electronics supply chains choosing between Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand.

body: Japan's response was the sharpest from a US ally on 26 Nov. Kihara rejected the premise that Japan runs non-market policies or holds structural excess production capacity and said the government had made its position known to Washington; Japan and the EU have both formally rejected the overcapacity finding.

Southeast Asian capitals were more measured. Thai government spokeswoman Lalida Persvivatana said the 18% cap was more favourable than expected and that Bangkok would keep pressing for competitive rates and product exemptions. Malaysia said it has no excess capacity distorting global markets and will keep consulting with the US. Singapore, facing up to 20%, repeated that it was very disappointed (AP, 26 Nov).

In Jakarta, Haryo Limanseto of the Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs said ministries would work with industry associations on public comments to secure product exemptions, while pointing to a comparative advantage over higher-tariffed competitors (26 Nov). USTR's case against Indonesia cites industrial policy, labour provisions, links to Chinese overcapacity, financial repression and the resource-downstreaming programme.

Beijing escalated its language between 25 and 26 Nov. After the foreign ministry called overcapacity a false premise, commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong said on 26 Nov that the announcement disrupts the international economic order and urged the US to return to dialogue; no countermeasures have been announced (as of 26 Nov).

stories.headline: Iran War, Day 273: IRGC Says a Laden Supertanker Is Burning After a Mine Strike Near Khasab, Kuwait Blames Tehran for Two Deaths, and Brent Settles at $96.57
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said on 26 Nov that two tankers hit mines and caught fire north of Oman's Khasab port on what it called an unauthorised route, one of them a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels; no vessels were named and the claim has not been independently confirmed. Kuwait said debris from intercepted Iranian drones killed two Italian technicians at an air-defence site on 26 Nov; Iran's military denied any operations in the region. ADNOC Logistics & Services said a Jordanian crew member missing since a 17 Nov attack on one of its vessels in the strait was found dead. US Treasury Secretary Bessent said Iran has run out of floating oil stocks and has loaded no tanker since the US blockade operation began in August, while envoy Kushner confirmed repeated meetings with Iranian officials. Brent settled $1.96 (2.1%) higher at $96.57 on 26 Nov, its third straight gain.
stories.market: Fresh mine claims and Houthi strikes on Saudi refineries pushed Brent up for a third session to $96.57 (26 Nov settle), about $7 above its 23 Nov low; tanker freight and war-risk cover, Gulf equities and Iran's rial are the channels to watch, while OPEC+'s 29 Nov meeting and a forecast surplus limit the rebound.

body: The IRGC navy reported a new pair of mine strikes on 26 Nov, this time north of Khasab on the Omani side of the strait. It said the two tankers had switched off their navigation systems and tried to pass covertly under US air cover, and that a supertanker with more than 2 million barrels aboard was left burning. Iran International noted the account rests only on the IRGC; no ship names, owners or independent confirmations have emerged. Gulf News separately reported that an outbound tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile about 33 km east of Khasab at 5 p.m. UAE time on 25 Nov, with all crew accounted for.

The human cost to Gulf states rose. Kuwait's defence ministry blamed 'Iranian aggression' after debris from intercepted drones killed two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia at an air-defence surveillance station on 26 Nov and wounded a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani; Iran's military spokesman denied any offensive operations and blamed Israel and US forces. The GCC secretary-general condemned the attack. ADNOC L&S confirmed that a Jordanian sailor missing since the 17 Nov attack on one of its ships had died; nine of 11 injured crew have been discharged.

Washington is leaning on economic pressure. Treasury Secretary Bessent said Iran has exhausted its floating crude stocks and has not loaded a tanker since 'Operation Economic Outcast' began in August, and Secretary of State Rubio said the blockade's damage means Trump no longer sees a need for a large military operation, according to Iran International. Inside Iran, truckers were on strike for a fifth day and the rial was at record lows. Kushner said Trump keeps 'all options on the table' and confirmed meetings with Iranian representatives within talks led by Vice President Vance; Tehran said Qatari and Pakistani mediators are still active.

Israel is pressing the other way: Netanyahu is reported to be lobbying for a renewed offensive and was due to convene his security cabinet on 26 Nov, and Israel said it is ready to strike Iran alone. Iran's foreign minister accused Israel of trying to pull the US into another war.

Traffic data are mixed. Vortexa figures reported by Bloomberg/gCaptain on 26 Nov show the seven-day average of crude, fuel and LNG carriers crossing the strait stayed above 26 a day through 19 Nov, up from below 25 on most October days, even as attacks rose; freight and insurance costs are near wartime highs. Brent settled at $96.57 on 26 Nov (+2.1%), with US crude inventories rising less than expected adding support; WTI traded near $84.84 without an official settlement because of Thanksgiving.

stories.headline: Houthi Strike on Aramco's 400,000-Barrel Jazan Refinery Kills a Worker and Halts Some Units, a Day After Ras Tanura Was Targeted
stories.summary: An aerial projectile hit Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on 26 Nov, killing a Nepali worker, injuring several others and temporarily halting some operations, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said; the Saudi-led coalition blamed the Houthis. The plant is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels a day, and the attack came a day after the Houthis claimed fires at Ras Tanura, the kingdom's largest refinery at 550,000 b/d, where Riyadh says it downed four drones. On 26 Nov Saudi defences also intercepted two ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh, two drones over the Eastern Province, a cruise missile aimed at the west and a drone near Jeddah port. The coalition said it destroyed the launcher used in Hodeidah province and vowed a 'firm military response'; Houthi media reported air strikes on Sanaa the same day.
stories.market: A confirmed hit on a Saudi refinery helped Brent to a third straight gain ($96.57, 26 Nov settle); with Hormuz largely shut, Saudi Red Sea ports and west-coast refineries are the kingdom's outlet, so product cracks, Red Sea war-risk cover and Saudi equities are the most exposed.

body: Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said an aerial projectile struck the Jazan refinery on the Red Sea coast on 26 Nov, starting a fire that killed a Nepali worker and injured several people of other nationalities. Some operations were halted temporarily while emergency and technical teams assessed the damage. The ministry did not name the attacker; the coalition said it was the Houthis, and later said it had destroyed a ballistic-missile launch platform in Hodeidah governorate used in the strike.

It is the first confirmed fatal hit on a Saudi energy plant in this round of fighting. On 25 Nov the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, on the Gulf coast, saying they caused fires; Riyadh said it shot down four drones over the site and has not confirmed damage, though The National said satellite images showed thick smoke. Ras Tanura's refining capacity is 550,000 b/d and Jazan's is up to 400,000 b/d.

The barrage continued on 26 Nov. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, two drones over the Eastern Province and a cruise missile heading for the western region were destroyed, along with a drone near Jeddah's port. The UAE condemned the attacks. Earlier in the week a Houthi strike on the PIF headquarters tower in Riyadh injured 11 people.

Fighting inside Yemen is widening. Houthi-affiliated media reported air strikes on Sanaa on 26 Nov; government forces said they carried out 767 strikes on Houthi positions that day and reported heavy clashes in Marib, al-Jawf and Taiz. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, which signed a mutual-defence pact in August, were due to discuss Yemen in Islamabad on 26 Nov.

stories.headline: Israeli Strikes Kill at Least Eight in Gaza Including a Senior Education Official, as Jets Hit a Hezbollah Rocket Site in the Beqaa
stories.summary: Israeli attacks killed at least eight Palestinians across Gaza on 26 Nov, including Khaled Abu Nada, undersecretary of the education ministry, and his wife in Deir el-Balah, health officials told Al Jazeera; Israel said he ran Hamas's economy and education portfolios. It was the third straight day Israel targeted Hamas officials, after the group's internal security chief and its northern Gaza security head. Gaza's health ministry says more than 1,600 people have been killed since the October 2025 truce, 130 of them this month. In Lebanon, the Israeli air force struck dozens of rockets and launchers at a Radwan Force camp near Ayn al-Tina in the Beqaa Valley on the evening of 26 Nov, with no injuries reported.
stories.market: Market impact is indirect: the Gaza strains weigh on Israel's coalition talks and defence budget and on Lebanon's distressed bonds, while Netanyahu's push for renewed strikes on Iran links the front to oil.

body: The 26 Nov strike in western Deir el-Balah killed Khaled Abu Nada and his wife and wounded six others; Netanyahu and Defence Minister Katz described him as a Hamas figure in charge of its economy and education files. Other attacks killed three people in Gaza City's Shati camp and three in the Tuffah district, health officials said.

The pattern of targeted killings has intensified this week: internal security director Naim Abu Nahl was killed on 24 Nov and northern Gaza security chief Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, with his wife and two daughters, on 25 Nov. Gaza's health ministry counts more than 1,600 killed and more than 6,000 wounded since the ceasefire took effect, and 74,746 killed since October 2023.

Diplomacy is stuck. The Board of Peace has set up a Palestinian technocratic administration to replace Hamas temporarily, but Netanyahu is blocking its phased disarmament plan as insufficient, and US envoy Kushner has urged Israel to drop its 'wartime mindset'. Netanyahu is also lobbying Washington for a new offensive against Iran, while opposition figure Eisenkot, who has until 6 Dec to form a government, says no immediate Iranian threat requires action.

On the northern front, the IDF said it struck rockets and launchers at a Radwan Force training camp near Ayn al-Tina in the Beqaa, about 25 km north of the border, on the evening of 26 Nov; Lebanese media reported large explosions. US Central Command said Syrian forces had seized IRGC-linked weapons bound for Lebanon.

stories.headline: Ukraine Hits the Slavyansk Refinery, a Transneft Pumping Hub and a Fertiliser-Plant Power Unit as Zelensky Warns a Russian Mass Strike on Energy Is Imminent
stories.summary: Ukrainian drones struck the Slavyansk-na-Kubani refinery in Krasnodar Krai overnight to 26 Nov, with its operator saying a crude distillation unit was seriously damaged and storage tanks pierced; Ukraine's military intelligence said the 5.2 million-tonne-a-year plant was still recovering from earlier strikes. The General Staff also claimed a hit on a Transneft oil pumping station in Bashkortostan, and drones targeted a power unit next to the Nevinnomyssk Azot fertiliser plant; Russia said it downed 343 drones. Zelensky said on 26 Nov that Russia is finishing preparations for a new mass attack on energy and logistics, after strikes killed 10 and injured 58 in a day and caused blackouts in 85 Mykolaiv settlements. Separately, a US-led consortium agreed on 25 Nov to take over Lukoil's foreign assets in a share swap that still needs US Treasury approval.
stories.market: Refinery and pipeline hits keep Russian product exports, and so European diesel, tight; TTF settled at €87.06 on 25 Nov and was near €87.75 on 26 Nov, with EU storage below 68% versus an 86% five-year norm leaving it sensitive to strikes on Ukraine's gas system. The Lukoil deal affects the Burgas, Zeeland and Petrotel refineries.

body: Ukraine kept up its long-range campaign against Russian energy overnight to 26 Nov. Slavyansk ECO, operator of the refinery in Krasnodar Krai, said drones seriously damaged one crude distillation unit, pierced storage tanks and started fires; local authorities reported four injured. Ukraine's military intelligence, which claimed the strike, put the plant's capacity at up to 5.2 million tonnes a year. Monitoring channels said the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara, hit on 25 Nov, was still burning on 26 Nov.

The General Staff said it also struck an oil station in Bashkortostan and an airfield in Volgograd region. A local official confirmed a fire at Transneft-Ural's Subkhankulovo pumping station, a junction on the trunk pipeline system with 10 tanks holding 160,000 cubic metres, blaming debris. In Stavropol Krai, drones targeted the industrial zone of Nevinnomyssk, and analysts identified a 410 MW power unit beside the EuroChem-owned Azot plant as the target. Russia's defence ministry said it downed 343 drones overnight.

Russia's strikes on Ukraine continued: overnight on 25 Nov it launched 113 drones, 87 of which were downed or suppressed, plus ballistic missiles that hit a Kyiv shopping centre, and attacks killed 10 and injured 58 over the day. Energy attacks caused temporary blackouts in 85 settlements in Mykolaiv region, and a large outage hit Russian-occupied Crimea. The IAEA said on 26 Nov it is negotiating a local ceasefire so both external lines to the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant can be repaired; the plant is on diesel generators after its 28th loss of off-site power in the war. stories.headline: Drone Strike on a Passenger Truck Kills 11 in West Kordofan as the UN Condemns the Blue Nile Attacks and Army Reinforcements Reach Damazin
stories.summary: A drone hit a truck carrying passengers and goods near Ghubeish in RSF-held West Kordofan on 26 Nov, killing at least 11 and wounding nine, a hospital source told AFP via Arab News; the RSF's political wing blamed the army. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric condemned the drone strikes on Ed Damazin and El Roseires that killed 17, saying civilians and infrastructure must never be targeted, and said OCHA has allocated nearly $36 million to Blue Nile this year. The army's 4th Infantry Division in Damazin announced the arrival of Sudan Shield Forces reinforcements as the RSF and SPLM-N press on several Blue Nile fronts. IOM said at least 795 people fled Abu Zabad in West Kordofan on 25 Nov.
stories.market: Sudan matters for markets mainly through gold output and smuggling, Red Sea trade via Port Sudan and power from the Roseires dam; global gold, which hit a 15-month intraday low of $3,445.89 on 25 Nov before recovering, is driven by US rates rather than the war.

body: The 26 Nov drone strike hit a vehicle travelling from Munam market to Ghubeish market in West Kordofan, which the RSF controls; the hospital source counted at least 11 dead and nine wounded. The RSF's political arm accused the army; there was no independent attribution. Drones are now the war's leading killer of civilians, with UN estimates putting drone deaths above 1,100 in the first half of 2026.

In Blue Nile, the UN said it was deeply concerned by the escalation and strongly condemned the strikes on Ed Damazin and El Roseires, which the Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative says killed 17 and injured 20. OCHA and partners have identified more than 6,700 newly displaced families at two sites in El Roseires needing food, water, health care and shelter; Dujarric said very significant funding gaps remain.

The army is reinforcing the state capital: its 4th Infantry Division said Sudan Shield Forces under Maj Gen Abu Agla Keikil had arrived to support operations, as the RSF and its SPLM-N allies advance on several fronts near the Ethiopian and South Sudanese borders. In Kordofan, IOM reported 795 people fleeing Abu Zabad on 25 Nov.

Other threads: four senior RSF commanders defected to the army in November, according to Sudanese media cited by The New Arab on 24 Nov, and EEPA reported unconfirmed claims that army chief Burhan approved sending Sudanese fighters to join Saudi-led operations against the Houthis, which neither Riyadh nor Yemen's government has confirmed.

stories.summary: Bank of Baroda expects India's economy to have grown 7.4% to 7.5% in the July-September quarter (Q2 FY27) and ICRA projects 7.5%, both above the Reserve Bank's own estimate for the period, Business Today reported on 27 Nov. The official GDP release is due on 30 Nov. Strong growth would land against inflation that rose to 6.1% in October from 5.5% in September, which RBI staff said on 25 Nov is broadening across categories. Most market watchers expect a 25-basis-point hike when the Monetary Policy Committee announces its decision on 4 Dec (consensus as of 26 Nov).
stories.market: A growth print above the RBI's estimate alongside 6%-plus inflation would reinforce hike expectations, a channel to short-dated government bond yields, rate-sensitive lenders and the rupee.

body: Early forecasts for the second quarter of fiscal 2026-27 cluster above 7%. Bank of Baroda's economists see growth of 7.4% to 7.5% and ICRA 7.5%; Business Today characterised both as running ahead of the RBI's projection for the quarter despite headwinds.

The data arrive at an awkward moment for the central bank. Headline CPI inflation reached 6.1% in October, up from 5.5% in September, and an RBI staff paper published on 25 Nov found that 11 of 12 consumption divisions recorded month-on-month increases and 11 states and union territories had inflation above 6%.

Solid activity removes one argument for caution on rates. Most market watchers expect the MPC to raise the policy rate by 25 basis points on 4 Dec, with the GDP release on 30 Nov the last major data point before the decision.

Separately, JPMorgan strategists said on 27 Nov they see 12% MSCI India earnings growth in calendar 2026 and 14% in 2027 (Business Today), a backdrop in which domestic demand rather than exports is doing the work.

stories.headline: Chips and Cars Escape the New US Tariffs, but Solar Modules, Storage Batteries and Inverters Do Not
stories.summary: An analysis by Shanghai Metals Market of the 25 Nov Section 301 notices finds that the exemption lists for China, India and five Southeast Asian economies include no solar cells or modules, and that lithium-ion batteries and inverters are exempt only for aircraft use (27 Nov). The 13 non-China proposals exempt goods already under Section 232 tariffs, such as semiconductors, cars, steel and copper, but polysilicon products are not on that list, so solar does not qualify automatically. Separate Section 232 polysilicon measures take effect on 4 Dec, with a 15% duty and minimum import prices of $0.38 per watt for modules and $0.22 for cells. Vietnam's cap would rise from 12.5% to 35% and India's from 10% to 25% under the proposals.
stories.market: The new duties add little for origins already carrying triple-digit anti-dumping and countervailing rates, such as India, but bite harder on storage batteries, inverters and suppliers with low existing duties, a cost question for US solar developers and battery-storage installers; origins outside the list, such as Laos and the Middle East, gain a relative edge.

body: Because the overcapacity tariffs apply to all goods except those listed in each economy's annexes, solar modules fall into scope whether or not solar is named in a country report. It is named in the China, India and Cambodia reports, and the China report lists batteries among 22 sectors of concern (SMM, 27 Nov).

The Section 232 carve-out in the 13 non-China proposals covers only goods currently subject to 232 tariffs, which today means steel, aluminium, copper, autos, lumber, patented pharmaceuticals and semiconductors. That shields chip and car imports from the new layer, but China's proposal has no such clause, and the polysilicon measures due on 4 Dec are not on the list.

For Indian modules the marginal effect is small next to anti-dumping duties of 123.04% and countervailing duties of 126.09% confirmed after the USITC's final determination on 14 Oct. Products and producers with low existing duties, notably storage batteries and inverters, face the most direct increase.

Rates could still move. If Vietnam, India and Singapore sign reciprocal deals, their caps would fall to 20%, 17% and 10%; if consultations fail, fallback rates reach 40% for China and 25% for Korea, Taiwan and several ASEAN states. Industry can ask for tariff-code exemption changes before the 5 Jan 2027 comment deadline, and Vietnam's trade ministry expects a final US decision between February and 11 March 2027.

stories.headline: US-Led Group With a Government Stake Agrees to Take Over Lukoil's Foreign Empire in a Share Swap That Sends No Cash to Russia
stories.summary: A consortium led by investment firm Eldridge, including the US International Development Finance Corporation, the UAE's Catena Investment Holding and Xtellus Partners, has agreed to buy Lukoil International GmbH, the sanctioned Russian company's non-Russian arm (26 Nov). The unit produces about 350,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day in 11 countries, owns refineries at Burgas, Zeeland and Petrotel with about 350,000 barrels a day of capacity, plus the LITASCO trading arm and more than 2,000 fuel stations in 16 countries. Lukoil will be paid in restricted shares of PJSC Lukoil and other Russian companies held in a custodial account for five years or until sanctions lift, and the DFC takes a stake on behalf of the US government at no upfront cost. The deal needs conditional OFAC approval and other regulatory clearances; no value was disclosed.
stories.market: The sale would end a year-long search for a buyer after late-2025 US sanctions and could bring idled refining capacity in Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Romania back to full runs, relevant for European diesel margins; Citi advised the buyers.

body: The structure is built to satisfy sanctions rules: Lukoil receives no cash, only restricted Russian equities parked in a custodial account, and Lukoil International will be fully separated from the Moscow parent at closing. The consortium said its first priority is stabilising operations, including restoring full refining capacity (World Oil, 26 Nov).
The DFC's stake makes the US government a direct part-owner of a global oil portfolio, which the buyers present as bringing the assets under American and allied ownership for energy-security reasons.

ExxonMobil, Chevron and ADNOC had all explored bids after the sanctions, and Carlyle held talks earlier in 2026. In Iraq, operatorship of West Qurna 2 passed from Lukoil to Basra Oil in February, and Baghdad has since agreed terms with Chevron, with signing targeted before year-end.
Closing depends on OFAC's conditional approval, due diligence and other regulators; no timetable or price has been published (as of 26 Nov).

stories.headline: Tata Trusts Take Tata Sons to the Bombay High Court to Undo Chandrasekaran's Reappointment, With a Hearing Set for Friday
stories.summary: Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and RD Tata Trust, the two largest of the charities that together own more than two-thirds of Tata Sons, moved the Bombay High Court (26 Nov) to have the 17 September board resolution reappointing N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for five more years declared invalid. They argue Article 121 of Tata Sons' articles needs the affirmative backing of the trust-nominated directors, which was missing because Noel Tata voted against and Venu Srinivasan in favour, and that chairman-of-the-meeting Harish Manwani's casting vote cannot override that. The suits also seek an order barring casting votes in such deadlocks and ₹65 crore in damages plus 18% annual interest. A bench headed by Justice Ahuja is due to hear the case at 3 pm IST on 27 Nov, ahead of a Tata Sons board meeting on 30 Nov.
stories.market: Tata group shares were mixed on 26 Nov: by early afternoon TCS was up about 2.6% at ₹2,582 and Tata Steel up about 2.1%, while Tata Motors fell about 2.8% to ₹429 and Trent and Indian Hotels slipped over 1% (NSE, about 13:55 IST). The fight bears on whether Tata Sons lists its shares, which the RBI said on 16 Nov is the way to meet rules for large non-bank lenders.

body: The dispute is the sharpest break yet between India's biggest conglomerate and the charitable trusts that control it. At the 17 September board meeting the two trust nominees split: Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, opposed a third term for Chandrasekaran and Venu Srinivasan backed it. Manwani treated the vote as tied and used his casting vote, and the board approved a new five-year term from 21 February 2027. The trusts said on 20 September that the resolution had no legal effect; Tata Sons maintains it was validly passed.

The petitions, mentioned in court by senior advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi, name Tata Sons, Chandrasekaran and five other directors; no relief is sought against Noel Tata. Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, holding 113,067 Tata Sons shares, seeks ₹50 crore and RD Tata Trust, with 8,838 shares, ₹15 crore. The case was first listed before Justice Arif Doctor, who recused himself, and moved to a bench headed by Justice Ahuja. The trusts are not seeking to stop the 30 November board meeting but want their voting rights observed there.

The trustees are divided too. Noel Tata, Neville Tata and Bhaskar Bhat voted for legal action under a 25 November circular, while Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh opposed; Singh has asked the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner to scrutinise the use of charitable funds for the litigation and to cap its cost pending a review.

Behind the boardroom clash is the question of a Tata Sons listing. The board also backed going public at the September meeting over Noel Tata's objection, and the Reserve Bank of India reiterated on 16 November that Tata Sons must meet the rules for upper-layer non-bank lenders, with a listing the way forward. Noel Tata wants the 30 November meeting to discuss restructuring options that keep Tata Sons private, a funding request from the Shapoorji Pallonji group, which owns more than 18%, and conflict-of-interest questions he has raised.
Brokers quoted on 26 Nov said the battle is unlikely to affect day-to-day operations at listed group companies, though it could shape the group's long-term direction.

stories.headline: Robinhood Loses Bid to Force Sports-Contract Gambling Claims Into Arbitration
stories.summary: US District Judge Edward Chen in San Francisco refused (25 Nov) Robinhood's request to send 10 of 11 plaintiffs in four consolidated cases to private arbitration. The customers are trying to recover losses on Robinhood's sports event contracts under state gambling laws. Chen held that Robinhood's arbitration agreements covered contracts regulated by the CFTC but not the sports contracts at issue; the eleventh plaintiff, from Michigan, had never accepted the agreement. He did not rule on the merits.
stories.market: The decision keeps a public court fight alive over Robinhood's (HOOD) prediction-market business as states and federal regulators clash over sports event contracts. A pending petition from New Jersey asks the US Supreme Court to take up the question, which could reshape the sector, including rival Kalshi.

body: The four cases were consolidated in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Plaintiffs say the sports contracts amount to illegal wagering under state law and want their losses back.

Robinhood argued its customer agreements send such disputes to arbitration. Chen found the clauses were written around CFTC-regulated contracts and did not reach these sports products, so the claims stay in open court. He left aside the plaintiffs' separate argument that the arbitration terms were unconscionable.

The parties have two weeks to file a status report proposing a schedule for an amended complaint and saying whether the case should be paused while the Supreme Court considers New Jersey's petition on whether states can police federally registered event contracts.

timeline.text: A New York state judge declines to immediately halt Kalshi's sports markets and asks for safeguards for 18- to 21-year-olds; three appeals courts this year sided with states and one with Kalshi.

stories.headline: 42 State Attorneys General Move to Block Character.AI's Auction of Chats From 21 Million US Accounts
stories.summary: A coalition of 42 state attorneys general led by California's Rob Bonta has asked the US Bankruptcy Court in Delaware to block bankrupt chatbot company Character.AI from selling its platform and user data, or at least the chat histories, at an auction set for 1 December (reported 25 Nov). The data cover more than 21 million US accounts, including over 2.1 million belonging to minors. The only disclosed bidder is Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, a Delaware company formed on 13 Nov, backed by New York-based Octave Advisors and named base bidder the next day. The states also oppose a $350,000 break-up fee and say a buyer would not be bound by Character.AI's privacy promises.
stories.market: The case tests whether user data can be monetised as an asset in AI-company bankruptcies; Walt Disney (DIS) has a separate $20 million licensing deal for Character.AI's IP, without user chats, still awaiting court approval, and Alphabet (GOOGL) holds a non-exclusive licence to its technology.

body: Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 protection in October. Its proposed sale process would put the chat histories of millions of users, along with data such as IP addresses, up for auction.

The attorneys general argue the company previously told users their data would not be sold, that a buyer could resell it without disclosure, and that the company has given the court less information on safety and legal risks than it gave bidders. They also point to new chatbot-safety laws in California, Colorado, New York and Connecticut taking effect on 1 January 2027. Bonta said any sale must exclude children's chats and other sensitive data.

Disney has offered $20 million for a non-exclusive licence to Character.AI's intellectual property and has hired its chief executive, Karandeep Anand, as its first chief technology officer, while offering jobs to close to 70 former staff. A similar coalition of states has objected to that deal as well. Co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas returned to Google after it licensed the startup's technology.

stories.headline: EU Top Court Says Amazon's Italian Delivery Units May Need a Postal Licence, Reviving AGCOM's 2018 Fines
stories.summary: The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled (26 Nov) that Amazon Italia Logistica, Amazon Italia Transport and Amazon Italia Services may need a general postal authorisation in Italy if their handling of third-party sellers' parcels counts as a postal service. The case stems from fines Italy's communications regulator AGCOM imposed in 2018 for providing postal services without authorisation, which the companies challenged. The court said Italy may require authorisation if it is justified by essential requirements such as data protection and is proportionate, and left the classification to Italy's Council of State.
stories.market: The ruling could add licensing and regulatory costs to Amazon's (AMZN) in-house delivery network in Italy and gives other EU postal regulators an argument for similar rules on marketplace logistics.

body: Italy's Council of State asked Luxembourg whether Amazon's activity as an intermediary delivering goods sold by third parties on its marketplace falls under the EU Postal Services Directive. The court answered under Articles 2 and 9 of Directive 97/67/EC that it can, depending on the facts.

An Advocate General opinion in July 2026 had taken a similar line, describing the services as part of the postal cycle. The Italian court must now decide whether the three Amazon units are postal providers and whether Italy's authorisation requirement is justified and proportionate.

stories.headline: Judge Bars the FCC From Its Early Review of Disney's Eight ABC Station Licences, Calling Retaliation 'Not a Close Case'
stories.summary: US District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington granted Disney and ABC a preliminary injunction (25 Nov) that stops the Federal Communications Commission from taking any further step in its early review of the licences of eight ABC-owned TV stations, including those in New York, Los Angeles and Chicago. In a 45-page opinion she found the companies likely to win their First Amendment retaliation claim and denied the FCC's motion to dismiss. The FCC ordered the review in April 2026, a day after President Trump called for Jimmy Kimmel's firing, although the licences were not due for renewal until October 2028 at the earliest. The FCC called the ruling wrong on the facts and the law; it must report compliance to the court by 2 December.
stories.market: The injunction removes, for now, the threat of a licence-revocation hearing over Walt Disney's (DIS) owned-and-operated stations, a core part of its linear TV business. US markets were shut for Thanksgiving on 26 Nov, so the first trading reaction comes in Friday's half-day session.

body: Disney and ABC sued the FCC and the administration in August 2026, arguing the early licence review was punishment for the network's programming. Judge AliKhan of the US District Court for the District of Columbia agreed the claim was strong, writing that it was no coincidence the review came one day after the president criticised Kimmel, and that FCC Chairman Brendan Carr appeared to treat the president's rhetoric as instructions.

The order bars the commission from any continuing or further action tied to the early renewal review, which means no hearing that could have led to the stations losing their licences. The judge noted that the FCC had not used this tool in more than half a century and treated the chilling effect on ABC's speech as irreparable harm.

The opinion also pointed to changes in how ABC's daytime show The View handled political guests during the midterm campaign, as the FCC is separately examining whether equal-time rules apply to it. Disney said the show invited no candidates before the November elections because of that inquiry.

The ruling does not halt a separate FCC investigation into Disney's employment practices. The FCC said it would keep using its lawful authority over broadcasters, while Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez welcomed the decision. The FCC can appeal to the DC Circuit.

stories.headline: Korean Watchdog's Staff Seek Up to 53.6 Billion Won Fine From Apple Over iPhone 16 AI Advertising
stories.summary: The Korea Fair Trade Commission's examiner sent the commission a report (24 Nov, announced 26 Nov) proposing to fine Apple up to 53.6 billion won, about $40 million, for allegedly deceptive advertising of AI features on the iPhone 16. The examiner says four of nine promoted features, including Genmoji, Image Playground and Siri's grasp of personal context, were not delivered as advertised, and that Apple changed its website wording without clearly telling buyers of delays. The proposed base fine of 26.8 billion to 53.6 billion won equals 0.8-1.6% of an estimated 3.35 trillion won of related sales. Apple disagrees and will argue its case before the full commission.
stories.market: The sum is small for Apple (AAPL), but it lands amid US complaints that Korean regulators target American tech firms, a point Washington has tied to possible Section 301 trade action.

body: The examiner also recommended a corrective order and a public notice. The findings do not bind the commission, and the final fine could be lower or, if the conduct is judged very serious, higher than 53.6 billion won.

According to the KFTC, Apple said at the September 2024 launch that the features would first arrive in US English by the end of 2024, changed its site about a month later to say the service was available, and in February 2025 promised Korean support by early April 2025. Siri's personal-context feature only launched in US English in September 2026 and in Korean in October 2026.

Apple says it cooperated fully, points to Korean-language Apple Intelligence support and dozens of features, and will present its position during deliberations. In October the Korea Communications Commission separately fined Apple 20.81 billion won over app-market practices.

stories.headline: Binance Fully Lifts Its Withdrawal Freeze Four Weeks After the $6.3 Billion North Korea-Linked Hack, as Washington Moves to Forfeit $1.1 Billion
stories.summary: Binance said on 26 Nov that it had fully ended the withdrawal suspension imposed after the 29 Oct theft of about $6.3 billion in assets, the largest crypto hack on record; a few networks remain paused for what it called unrelated maintenance. The exchange says it replaced customer losses from company funds and its SAFU reserve, reporting 98% restored by 3 Nov. The FBI and TRM Labs attribute the attack to the North Korean group TraderTraitor; Pyongyang denies involvement. On 23 Nov the US Justice Department filed to permanently forfeit more than $1.1 billion in USDC from the haul, and US officials say more than $2.9 billion has been frozen, seized or returned.
stories.market: The end of the freeze removes an overhang on the world's largest exchange and its BNB token, while the record seizure underlines stablecoin issuers' ability to freeze stolen funds, a factor for Circle and Tether's compliance profile.

body: Binance's announcement on Thursday 26 Nov closes the operational chapter of a breach that began on 29 Oct, when attackers gained access to part of its systems and pushed out unapproved withdrawals. The exchange halted withdrawals on several blockchains the same day and restarted them in stages from 1 Nov, beginning with bitcoin.

In a 3 Nov report Binance said the intruders combined fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to reach the systems that control its wallets; its initial finding pointed to a compromised engineer's laptop. Co-CEO Yi He pledged to cover all losses, and Binance has set aside about $6.34 billion for that purpose.

Law enforcement has moved unusually fast. US investigators froze part of the funds within minutes, and Circle and Tether froze stablecoins linked to the theft. The Justice Department's civil forfeiture filing on Monday 23 Nov targets more than $1.1 billion in USDC already under a restraining order; US officials put total freezes, seizures and returns above $2.9 billion, up from $2.7 billion on 12 Nov. Binance also won a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic estimates about $2.85 billion is frozen and roughly $2.35 billion still sits in theft-linked addresses, with at least $247 million moved through bitcoin mixing transactions, according to Decrypt. Binance has warned customers that scammers typically target users after such incidents.

stories.headline: BitMart Discloses a $319 Million Hole With $1.9 Million in Liquid Assets, as London Approves a £55 Million Recovery in Singapore's Biggest Laundering Case
stories.summary: Crypto exchange BitMart has reportedly told restructuring adviser Alvarez & Marsal it faces a $319.5 million shortfall with only $1.9 million in liquid assets available to repay customers, Cointelegraph reported on 26 Nov, citing Nikkei Asia. Many affected users are Chinese investors drawn by short-term savings products paying 18.8% annualised on 14-day deposits, and numerous users say they cannot access accounts. Separately, a UK court approved a £55 million asset-recovery settlement from Su Haijin and Xu Haika, defendants in Singapore's largest money-laundering case, with Xu required to sell 16 London apartments. The US Justice Department also publicised a nationwide fraud surge of more than 400 criminal cases and over 800 defendants targeting crypto investment scams and laundering networks.
stories.market: A deep shortfall at a mid-tier exchange revives counterparty worries over high-yield crypto 'earn' products and could weigh on smaller exchange tokens; recoveries in the Singapore case show cross-border asset tracing is reaching property markets.

stories.headline: Mahanadi Coalfields Lists 1.5% Below Its Issue Price in the First Big Debut Since SEBI Told Intermediaries to Stop Publishing Grey-Market Premiums
stories.summary: Mahanadi Coalfields, Coal India's ₹8,981 crore offer-for-sale, opened at ₹134 on NSE on 27 Nov, 1.47% below its ₹136 issue price, and at ₹133.15 on BSE (-2.1%), leaving retail holders about ₹220 down per 110-share lot at the NSE open. Unofficial premiums had already fallen to zero before the debut after the issue drew only 1.52 times demand, with retail at 0.46 times. It is the first major listing since SEBI's 24 Nov advisory asking registered intermediaries to stop publishing, displaying or circulating grey-market premium (GMP) figures, on the grounds that such trades are unregulated and lack settlement guarantees. Foodlink F&B Holdings' ₹360.76 crore IPO was 1.08 times subscribed on day one (26 Nov), with retail at 2.33 times.
stories.market: A below-issue debut for the season's largest PSU offer may cool appetite for upcoming state disinvestments; Coal India (COALINDIA) and newly listed MAHACOAL are in focus, and the GMP curb removes a widely watched, if unreliable, sentiment gauge.

body: Mahanadi Coalfields' issue was a pure offer for sale of 66.18 crore shares, a 10% stake, by parent Coal India, priced at the top of a ₹129-136 band. Subscription closed on 23 Nov at 1.52 times, with institutional buyers at about 4.9 times but non-institutional demand at 66% and retail at 46%.

The flat grey market before listing proved a better guide than for Crystal Crop Protection, which on 26 Nov listed at ₹278, about 2.2% above its ₹272 issue price and below its last quoted premium. Watrana Rentals also opened 0.82% below its ₹245 issue price this week, Business Upturn reported.

SEBI's advisory, issued on Monday 24 Nov according to news reports, covers websites, digital platforms, email, SMS and social media. The regulator said grey-market trades sit outside the exchange system, that investors in them have no recourse to exchange grievance mechanisms, and that reported premiums had diverged from listing prices in several recent large IPOs. No penalties were announced.

Demand for the issue itself was lukewarm: the Rs 8,981.12 crore offer, a pure offer for sale of 66.18 crore shares (a 10% stake) by Coal India, was subscribed 1.52 times overall, with institutions bidding 4.95 times their portion but retail investors taking up only 46% of theirs. Anchor investors led by LIC had been allotted Rs 2,295.2 crore of stock before the issue opened.

stories.headline: Rial Slides Toward 3 Million per Dollar on Tehran's Street Market, Nearly 50% Weaker Than the Central Bank's Official Rate
stories.summary: The US dollar was quoted at about 2.93-2.96 million rials on Iran's unofficial market on 26 Nov, extending the record low of just over 2.9 million set on 25 Nov, while the euro fetched about 3.21-3.24 million, Trend news agency reported. The Central Bank of Iran's official rate for the same day was 1,959,682 rials per dollar, meaning the street dollar costs roughly 50% more. Pressure has built since US Treasury sanctions on 23 Nov against 22 entities and 8 people in an Iranian network of exchange houses, on top of a US naval blockade that has squeezed oil exports.
stories.market: The street rate is the most immediate gauge of sanctions and blockade pressure on Iran; it tracks Hormuz risk premiums in Brent and secondary-sanctions exposure for Gulf money-service businesses.

stories.headline: Nigeria Lets Banks Sell Up to $1 Million in Cash to Bureaux de Change to Ease Street-Market Pressure; Argentina's Blue Dollar Holds at 1,710
stories.summary: Nigeria's central bank allowed banks from 25 Nov to sell up to $1 million in physical cash to bureau-de-change operators, against a previous cap of $150,000 a week of which only 25% could be taken in notes, aiming to ease pressure on the parallel market, Nairametrics reported. Street quotes for the naira varied by tracker on 26 Nov, from about ₦1,437 to ₦1,460 per dollar, against an official NFEM close of ₦1,397 on 25 Nov, near nine-month lows. In Argentina, the informal 'blue' dollar closed unchanged at 1,690/1,710 pesos on 26 Nov after a jump the day before, about 5% above the official Banco Nación selling rate of 1,625, with country risk at 1,067 basis points, Perfil reported.
stories.market: Nigeria's cash release targets the gap between official and street naira rates that typically widens at year-end; in Argentina a narrow blue-official gap suggests the parallel market is not signalling a disorderly break, while a country-risk spread above 1,000 bp keeps sovereign bonds under pressure.

body: The Central Bank of Nigeria notified banks of the change by email, according to Nairametrics, and is expected to supply extra cash liquidity where needed. Governor Olayemi Cardoso has attributed recent naira weakness to seasonal year-end portfolio adjustments, corporate hedging and election-related spending, and said he expects volatility to ease in 2027, citing remittances of nearly $1.9 billion in the preceding month.

The street dollar has climbed from about ₦1,375 a month ago to roughly ₦1,455-1,460, while the official central rate rose about 2.1% between 18 and 25 Nov. Gross reserves stood at about $54.25 billion on 24 Nov. Street quotes come from online trackers rather than confirmed dealer prices.

In Buenos Aires the blue dollar was steady on Thursday after a rise on Wednesday; the MEP rate stood near 1,671 and the CCL near 1,768 pesos, per Perfil. The blue has gained 145 pesos in November from 1,565 at end-October, El Cronista reported, and the wholesale rate remains well below the top of the official band at 1,982.89.

stories.headline: Thousands Protest in Erbil Against Baghdad's Anti-Smuggling Takeover, as Officials Put Diverted Crude at Up to 230,000 Barrels a Day
stories.summary: Thousands of people, tens of thousands according to Kurdistan24, protested in Erbil on 26 Nov against the federal government's move to take over the Kurdish region's border crossings and oil exports, which Baghdad justifies as an anti-smuggling drive. Iraqi government figures cited by Al Jazeera put smuggled oil at 200,000-230,000 barrels per day, worth about $200 million a month. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's 24 Nov orders also dismissed eight officials, including the head of the Border Ports Authority, and Iraq's top court upheld federal control of borders and oil exports within 24 hours. Baghdad denied reports of troops moving toward the region, and the country's four presidencies agreed to a national dialogue on 1 Dec.
stories.market: A durable federal crackdown could curb leakage of Iraqi crude into grey channels serving sanctioned Iran, but the Baghdad-Erbil standoff adds risk to northern exports and Kurdistan-focused oil producers.

body: The government's smuggling estimate, if accurate, would equal a significant share of Iraq's northern output. Officials also claim tens of billions of dollars have ended up in private accounts over the years, an allegation Kurdish authorities have not accepted.

A leaked federal intelligence report published on 25 Nov described crude from Kirkuk being trucked through Kurdistan into Iran, relabelled and sold on in Afghanistan, with a second route toward the Turkish border using reissued shipping papers.

The dispute builds on a February 2022 Supreme Court ruling that the Kurdish region's oil and gas law was unconstitutional, the 2023 halt of the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline and the interim deal under which Kurdish exports resumed in September 2025. Baghdad has said Kurdish public-sector salaries will be secured in the 2027 budget.

stories.headline: France Releases Sanctioned Tanker DF Peak After Its Owner Pleads Guilty Over a False Flag and Forfeits a Reported €1 Million
stories.summary: A court on Réunion convicted the owner of the crude tanker DF Peak on 24 Nov under a guilty-plea procedure for failing to justify the ship's nationality, and the confiscation penalty, reportedly about €1 million, has been paid, Marine Insight reported on 26 Nov. The 2007-built vessel, linked in maritime reports to Russia's Sovcomflot and sanctioned by the EU, US, UK and others, had claimed Benin's flag despite being deregistered. French naval forces boarded it on 12 Oct more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion; it was the fifth suspected shadow-fleet tanker intercepted by France in 2026. The release comes as EU governments weigh a 22nd sanctions package that would add more than 70 vessels to the shadow-fleet list and ban tankers insured in Russia.
stories.market: Rising boardings and prosecutions raise the cost and risk of moving Russian crude outside Western insurance and flag systems, supporting freight rates on compliant tankers and widening the legal exposure of shadow-fleet operators.

body: The DF Peak, renamed from Kaliningrad in June 2024 and transferred to a Hong Kong-registered company, was escorted to Réunion and held from 14 Oct with its 21 crew aboard under French military supervision. The prefect will lift the detention order and French authorities will monitor the ship until it leaves French jurisdiction; the owner says it is seeking a new flag.

France relied on Article 110 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which allows warships to inspect a vessel suspected of having no nationality. Russia's embassy in France called the interception piracy, arguing the article does not permit diversion or detention.

EU forces used the same legal basis on 13 Nov to board the tanker Midag south of Malta, confirming a false Zimbabwe flag before letting it continue. The 22nd package, announced by Ursula von der Leyen on 23 Nov, also targets repair services for Russian refineries and needs unanimous approval from the 27 member states.

stories.headline: Mexican Customs Seizes 18 Million Counterfeit Cigarettes at Lázaro Cárdenas in a Market Where One in Four Smokes Is Illegal
stories.summary: Mexican customs, the navy and the security ministry seized more than 18 million counterfeit cigarettes in two containers at the Pacific port of Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán, earlier this week, Mexico News Daily reported on 26 Nov; one shipment, of about 8.3 million cigarettes, came from Singapore. The cargo has been handed to the Federal Attorney General's Office. A KPMG study commissioned by Philip Morris International found 23.3% of cigarettes consumed in Mexico in 2025, about 9.2 billion sticks, were illegal, costing an estimated $1.3 billion in lost tax.
stories.market: Illicit volumes erode legal sales and excise revenue for tobacco majors such as Philip Morris International (PM) and British American Tobacco (BATS), and for Mexico's federal budget.

stories.headline: Goldman Sells $1.5 Billion of Loans From a Shrinking Private BDC at 94.75 Cents, Giving Private Credit a Rare Market Price
stories.summary: Goldman Sachs has priced a GP-led secondary sale of about $1.5 billion of assets from its non-traded Goldman Sachs Private Middle Market Credit II at 94.75, led by Coller EQT with a $200-300 million commitment and the rest syndicated, PitchBook reported via FinancialMarkets.com on 25 Nov. The fund's total assets have fallen to $1.38 billion from $1.88 billion a year earlier, NAV per share is down 14% to $65.20, and $97.3 million of principal at four companies is on non-accrual; a JPMorgan credit facility is due to end on 15 Jan 2027. The price is close to the fund's own carrying value of 94.2 cents on cost at 30 June, but its exact basis is undisclosed. The deal lands as investors await early-December redemption data from the biggest non-traded private-credit funds.
stories.market: An observable price near book eases fears that private-credit marks are inflated, but non-accruals and shrinking assets keep pressure on BDC discounts to NAV and listed managers such as GS, BX, OWL and ARES.

body: The portfolio is 98% first-lien loans across 56 borrowers, valued as of 31 March. Evercore advised; Goldman, Coller and Evercore declined to comment, according to the report.

Like the roughly $4 billion collateralised fund obligation that New York State's Common Retirement Fund is weighing, backed by stakes in about 20 private-credit funds including Blackstone and Blue Owl vehicles, the sale creates liquidity through structure rather than a deep-discount fire sale.

Valuation dispersion remains a concern: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management research published in early November found the share of borrowers whose marks differ by at least 5 points across BDC managers rose to 12.3% at 30 June from 9.3% a year earlier, and about one in ten BDC loans is valued below 90% of face.

stories.headline: Imperial Brands Has Its Best Day Since 1999, Up 13%, as Altria Weighs an All-Cash Bid and Japan Tobacco Circles
stories.summary: Altria said on 26 Nov it is considering a possible offer for Imperial Brands that would likely be solely in cash, and that it is in talks with an unnamed third party about buying part of Imperial's business, with no agreement yet. Bloomberg reported Japan Tobacco has been working with advisers on a possible deal, potentially splitting Imperial's assets by region with another buyer. Imperial shares rose as much as 17.6% to 3,562p and closed 13.3% higher at 3,432p (26 Nov close), the highest since July 2017. Imperial said it had received no approach but would consider any proposal. Under UK takeover rules Altria has until 24 Dec to make a firm offer or walk away. Japan Tobacco rose about 4% in Tokyo on Friday afternoon (27 Nov).
stories.market: A bid would be the largest tobacco takeover in a decade at an Imperial market value near £26 billion; the rally lifted European staples, while Japan Tobacco outpaced a 1.8% TOPIX gain on 27 Nov and Altria's shares were indicated about 2% higher ahead of Friday's shortened US session.

body: Altria, the Marlboro maker that sells only in the US, confirmed on 26 Nov that it is weighing a possible offer for Imperial Brands, the London-listed owner of brands such as Winston in the US and Davidoff internationally. It said any bid would likely be in cash and that it is discussing with an unnamed third party a purchase of part of Imperial's business; no agreement has been reached and there is no certainty an offer will be made.

Bloomberg had reported that Japan Tobacco is evaluating an acquisition of Imperial, possibly with a partner, which would allow the assets to be carved up by geography. Japan Tobacco declined to comment. Imperial said it had not received any approach or proposal but would consider one if it came.

Imperial shares jumped as much as 17.6% to 3,562p intraday, giving a market value of about £26.8 billion, before closing up 13.3% at 3,432p, their best day since December 1999 and highest close since July 2017 (26 Nov). Reuters cited LSEG data showing that, at a premium, a deal would be the third-largest takeover of a tobacco company on record and the biggest in the sector in a decade; BAT's 2016 purchase of Reynolds American was about $60 billion including debt.

Japan Tobacco shares were up about 4% in Friday afternoon trade in Tokyo (27 Nov), against a 1.8% rise in the TOPIX. The company had about ¥887.3 billion of cash at the end of September and recently booked a ¥1.4 trillion charge that leaves it forecasting a full-year operating loss of ¥368 billion.

Analysts focused on structure. RBC Capital Markets said a joint Altria-Japan Tobacco approach could ease antitrust objections because Altria operates only in North America. Jefferies said a deal could make JT a sizeable third-place US competitor with cost-saving potential, and BTIG said it could likely be financed without hurting either buyer's credit ratings, partly by reissuing JT treasury shares worth about $7.4 billion.

detail.consensus: Analysts see a region-by-region carve-up as the most plausible structure, with antitrust and financing considered manageable.

stories.headline: Schaeffler's Parent Sells 6.5% of Its Indian Unit for Rs 3,549 Crore, and the Stock Rises Anyway
stories.summary: German group Schaeffler, through Schaeffler Schweinfurt Beteiligungs GmbH, sold 1.016 crore Schaeffler India shares, about 6.49%, at an average Rs 3,493 in block deals on 26 Nov, raising Rs 3,548.79 crore. Domestic and foreign institutions bought equal amounts. The price was about 3% below the prior close, yet the shares rose as much as 4.73% to Rs 3,775 (26 Nov). Combined promoter holding fell to 67.64% from 74.13%. In a separate block the same day, 47.37 lakh Amagi Media shares (2.15%) changed hands at Rs 554 for Rs 262.44 crore, while LG Electronics is selling up to 2% of its Indian unit through Citi and HSBC.
stories.market: Three large promoter-side sales in two days were absorbed without heavy discounts, a sign of deep domestic and foreign institutional demand while foreign investors are net buyers; the Schaeffler sale also widens the stock's free float.

body: Exchange disclosures published after the 26 Nov session confirmed that Schaeffler Schweinfurt Beteiligungs GmbH, a Schaeffler AG entity, sold 1,01,59,738 shares of Schaeffler India at an average Rs 3,493, a deal worth Rs 3,548.79 crore. Its own stake fell to 20.79% from 27.28%, taking combined promoter holding to 67.64% from 74.13%, just above two-thirds. Domestic and foreign institutions bought equal numbers of shares.

The sale price was roughly 3% below the previous close of about Rs 3,600, but the stock climbed as much as 4.73% to Rs 3,775 intraday, as investors treated the larger free float and index-weight implications as positives.

Amagi Media Labs also saw a block of 47.37 lakh shares, 2.15% of equity, at Rs 554, about 3% below the prior close, for Rs 262.44 crore; the shares edged 0.83% higher to Rs 576 (26 Nov). Sellers and buyers were not named.

LG Electronics' sale of up to 13.58 million shares, 2% of LG Electronics India, at a floor of Rs 1,709.30 is being run by Citigroup and HSBC and is worth about 370 billion won ($250 million). A full sale cuts the parent to 83%; it must reach a 75% maximum by October 2030 under Indian float rules.

stories.headline: Tata Steel Signals It May Rework the APL Apollo Deal After a 30% Two-Day Rout in the Target's Shares
stories.summary: Tata Steel chief executive T. V. Narendran said on 26 Nov the two companies are looking at changes to the financial structure of their transaction after investors objected to its debt, funding and earnings effects. The deal announced on 23 Nov has Tata Steel buying the Gupta family's 26.4% of APL Apollo for up to Rs 15,510 crore and making an open offer for 26% more at Rs 2,301.40, while selling its tubes and colour-coated business to APL Apollo for Rs 28,000 crore. APL Apollo lost about 30% over two sessions and Tata Steel more than 10% since the announcement (25 Nov close). Both edged higher on 26 Nov morning, Tata Steel up 2.13% at Rs 162.70.
stories.market: Brokers' Tata Steel targets range from Rs 179 (JPMorgan) to Rs 241 (Macquarie), with no major rating changes, while APL Apollo drew rating cuts; any restructuring could ease the debt load the deal would shift onto APL Apollo.

body: Tata Steel's plan, unveiled on 23 Nov, would make it the controlling shareholder of APL Apollo, India's largest structural steel tube maker. It would buy the 26.4% held by chairman Sanjay Gupta's family for up to Rs 15,510 crore and launch a mandatory open offer for another 26% at Rs 2,301.40 a share, which could cost up to Rs 16,756 crore more.

In the other leg, Tata Steel would transfer its tubes business and Tata Steel Colors to APL Apollo for Rs 28,000 crore. Roughly Rs 10,000 crore of that would sit as debt on APL Apollo's balance sheet and about Rs 18,000 crore would convert into equity, raising concerns among analysts about higher interest costs at the target.

The market reaction was severe. APL Apollo fell nearly 12% on 25 Nov alone, taking its two-session loss to about 30%, and Tata Steel slid 2.3%, extending its post-deal fall past 10%. On 26 Nov Narendran said changes were being studied that would address the financial structure while keeping the strategic logic, without giving details; Gupta is weighing keeping some shares and investing more to show commitment.

Brokers mostly kept their Tata Steel targets well above the market: Jefferies and JM Financial at Rs 240, Macquarie Rs 241, UBS and Investec Rs 220, Centrum Rs 215 (Buy), MOFSL Rs 190 (Buy), Morgan Stanley Rs 185 and JPMorgan Rs 179.

stories.headline: Babcock Lands the Biggest Contract in Its History, an £8.7 Billion Submarine Support Deal, and Rises 6.5%
stories.summary: Britain's Ministry of Defence signed an £8 billion contract and a £700 million framework with Babcock International on 26 Nov to maintain and support Royal Navy submarines and run naval base services at Devonport and Clyde. The deal runs five years from early December and can be extended to as long as 15 years. It replaces the future maritime support programme, whose extension ends next week. Babcock shares closed 6.5% higher, leading the FTSE 100 (26 Nov), after touching 1,095p intraday.
stories.market: The award removes a renewal risk from Babcock's largest revenue stream and lifted UK defence names; the MoD says about £2.4 billion will be spent in the wider UK supply chain, roughly £1 billion of it with smaller firms.

body: The new arrangement is a single integrated framework covering submarine maintenance, engineering and technical services as well as naval base services at HMNB Devonport and HMNB Clyde, aimed at improving submarine availability for the UK's continuous at-sea nuclear deterrent.

Babcock said the work will safeguard 8,500 jobs and create 3,000 more. The MoD said about £2.4 billion of the spending will flow into the UK supply chain, with roughly £1 billion targeted at small and medium-sized businesses.

Shares rose 5.6% to 1,077.50p in early trade and as much as about 7% to 1,095p before closing up 6.5% (26 Nov). Citigroup's Charles Armitage said renewal had never been in much doubt but that a five-year term gives certainty.
